name: Australia (Commonwealth)
note: Deaths are registered by the eight State and Territory registries; there is no national population register. Commonwealth law reaches the chain at a few points: registrars must send monthly death lists to the Australian Electoral Commission, the Queensland registry pools all registries' deaths into national fact-of-death data for approved government agencies and, through the Australian Death Check, for approved private organisations. The registries also run the Australian Death Notification Service, a tell-once form for banks and utilities, and verify death certificates through the Document Verification Service. The Privacy Act does not protect the information of deceased persons.

steps.title: State registrar forwards monthly lists of registered deaths to the AEC
steps.who: The Registrar-General (registrar of births, deaths and marriages) of each State and Territory.
steps.trigger: Registration of the death of a person aged 16 or over.

deadline.text: as soon as practicable after the beginning of each month, for deaths registered in the preceding month

steps.summary: Commonwealth law obliges every State registrar to send the Electoral Commissioner a monthly list of the names, addresses, ages, sexes and dates of death of everyone 16 or over whose death it registered. Section 112 extends this to the territories.

steps.title: AEC removes the deceased elector from the roll
steps.trigger: Receipt of a registrar's death list under s 108.
steps.summary: On receiving the lists the Electoral Commissioner must alter the rolls; deceased electors are removed without the objection process required for other removals.

steps.title: National fact-of-death data supplied to approved government agencies
steps.who: State and territory registries supply death data to the Queensland Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, the coordinating registry, which gives approved applicants (Commonwealth and state agencies) national fact-of-death data (the Fact of Death Data Service).
steps.trigger: Registration of the death in any State or Territory.
steps.summary: There is no national population register; the national death dataset is assembled by the coordinating registry (Queensland BDM) from all registries and released to approved government users. The Fact of Death Data Service name and its recipient list could not be read on an official page.

steps.title: Services Australia (Centrelink, Medicare) learns of the death from registry data
steps.who: Services Australia, which administers Centrelink payments and Medicare.
steps.trigger: Registry death data received through the national fact-of-death data arrangement.
steps.summary: Services Australia states that it is told of deaths by registries but still asks families to tell it, particularly where the person was receiving payments. Its pages were unreachable in this pass, so this rests on the earlier DER reading only.

steps.title: Medicare enrolment closed on registry death data
steps.summary: Medicare is run by Services Australia and is understood to update enrolments from the same registry death data. No official text was readable.

steps.title: ATO notified of the death
steps.who: The executor or administrator (legal personal representative).
steps.trigger: The death; administration of the estate.
steps.summary: The ATO asks the legal personal representative to notify it of the death and can lodge inquiries with State registries, which the NSW Registry confirms. ato.gov.au refused this client, so the ATO guidance itself was not read.

steps.title: Passport cancelled on the holder's death
steps.who: The Minister (Australian Passport Office, Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade).
steps.trigger: The holder's death, known from registry data or a family report.
steps.summary: The Minister may cancel an Australian travel document when the holder dies. How the Passport Office learns of the death (registry data feed or family return of the passport) could not be read on an official page.

steps.title: Australian Death Check: organisations match their records against national registry death data
steps.who: Commercial and government organisations approved for access, through the Queensland Registry as coordinating registry (access via approved data-service brokers).
steps.trigger: The organisation submits its customer records for matching.
steps.summary: The Australian Death Check is the registries' joint service that lets approved organisations, including banks and insurers, check customer records against national fact-of-death data.

steps.title: Australian Death Notification Service tells nominated organisations
steps.who: A family member or executor uses the online service; the registry notifies the banks, utilities, telcos and other organisations nominated.
steps.trigger: The informant lodges a notification and nominates organisations.
steps.summary: A single official form, run by the state and territory registries, sends notice of the death to the organisations the family chooses.

steps.title: Document Verification Service confirms a presented death certificate
steps.who: Any government or private body that is a party to a DVS participation agreement.
steps.trigger: A person presents a death certificate and the organisation queries the issuing registry.
steps.summary: Death certificates are DVS documents, so a bank or insurer that participates in the DVS can check electronically that a certificate presented to it matches the registry's record. The registry answers each query.

centralPopulationRegister.note: No national population register. Death data is pooled by the Queensland Registry as coordinating registry from the State and Territory registers; the Electoral Act has each State registrar send death lists directly to the AEC.

governmentPropagation.note: Registration reaches the AEC by statute (s 108) and approved Commonwealth agencies through national fact-of-death data; Services Australia and the ATO still ask families or executors to tell them, and the agency pages could not be read.

privateSectorVerification.note: The Australian Death Check gives approved commercial organisations access to national fact-of-death data, and DVS lets participants verify a presented death certificate. The Privacy Act does not cover deceased persons' information (OAIC).

gaps: servicesaustralia.gov.au (curl exit 92 / WebFetch 503), my.gov.au, aec.gov.au, idmatch.gov.au, passports.gov.au, abs.gov.au, australiandeathcheck.gov.au, deathnotification.gov.au, qld.gov.au and sa.gov.au were blocked by egress policy; www.ato.gov.au answered 403 (origin refusal). The Services Australia, Medicare and ATO steps are therefore unverified.

Fact of Death Data Service (FODDS): the name, governance and list of Commonwealth recipients (Services Australia, ATO, DFAT, Home Affairs) were not found on a readable official page; only the NSW Registry's description of 'national fact of death data' via the Queensland coordinating registry was read.
Australian Death Check: the official site australiandeathcheck.gov.au and the Queensland Government national-data page were unreachable; access terms, broker list and data latency not confirmed.

No Commonwealth statute was found that obliges a registrar to notify Services Australia, Medicare, the ATO or the Passport Office; the feeds appear to rest on intergovernmental agreements and state registry information-sharing powers (e.g. Qld BDMR Act 2023 s 118).
Social Security (Administration) Act 1999 (Compilation No. 164) was searched for a death-notification duty; none found beyond general information-gathering powers (s 192).
No public-notice stage at Commonwealth level; deceased-estate notices are State law.
